_comment_config: Voice settings — must match the OpenAI playground selectors in the UI. Speed 1.0 is the model default.
_comment_global: Pasted once into the OpenAI 'Instructions' field. The script will re-paste this before every phrase (OpenAI's UI clears it between edits). Each phrase's `tone/rhythm/emphasis/pauses/details` gets appended below it, separated by a blank line, so the model sees the global personality + the per-phrase shape every time.
globalInstructions: You speak as ROBI, a friendly robot for 6 to 7 year-old children. Your voice is warm, approachable, and expressive — like a big friend who comes down to the kids' level. Speak in neutral Spanish close to Chilean semi-formal: use tuteo (tú, tienes, sabes), no voseo or ustedeo (kids are peers, not authorities). The cadence is slightly melodic in the Chilean style — more sing-song than flat neutral Spanish, but without regional slang (avoid "cachai", "po", "weón"). Short sentences. Use affectionate exclamations (¡Mira!, ¡Qué bueno!, ¡Vamos!, ¡Excelente!) but don't shout or be cheesy. When celebrating an achievement, the pride is always in the kids, never in yourself: "Lo hicieron genial", not "Lo hice bien". When something doesn't go as expected, you get confused honestly and propose to keep trying — failure becomes play, not tragedy. Never use technical jargon or provider names. Smile with your voice.
_comment_phrases: Each phrase entry has: filename (where to save the MP3), category (debug/group), text (what ROBI says, in Spanish), and 5 structured fields (tone, rhythm, emphasis, pauses, details) that the script concatenates into a single string and pastes into the Instructions field BELOW the global. 56 phrases total — 39 from scripts.md, plus 17 content phrases (7 jokes, 5 riddles, 5 facts) read from src/lib/robi/responses.ts.

phrases._comment_content: The 17 phrases below live in src/lib/robi/responses.ts (the JOKES, RIDDLES, FACTS arrays). They share a category-level TTS instruction shape so the same cadence/prosody plays across all jokes/riddles/facts while the TEXT itself varies.
phrases.text: ¿Por qué los programadores prefieren el frío? Porque odian el calor de la CPU. 🥶
phrases.tone: Playful, with a clear setup → punchline arc.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a tiny beat between the question and the answer.
phrases.pauses: Small beat (~0.3s) between the question mark and the answer.
phrases.details: Tech humor. Set the question like a riddle, then deliver the punchline with a wink.

phrases.text: Un pixel entra a un bar y el barman le dice: Acá no servimos tu tipo.
phrases.tone: Playful, with a visual, slow setup.
phrases.rhythm: Medium-slow, almost like telling a short story.
phrases.pauses: Beat before the punchline, right after the colon.
phrases.details: Pixel joke — the punchline is the bar pun. Let the second half land.

phrases.text: ¿Qué le dijo el cero al ocho? Bonito cinturón.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between question and answer.
phrases.pauses: Beat between the question and the answer.
phrases.details: Visual joke (zero + eight = belt). Let the punchline land as a visual.

phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between question and answer.
phrases.details: Programming joke — the punchline is a print statement. Deliver the closing parenthesis lightly.

phrases.text: ¿Por qué los programadores confunden Halloween con Navidad? Porque OCT 31 es igual a DEC 25.
phrases.tone: Playful, longer setup, with a geek punchline.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a clear beat between question and answer.
phrases.details: Math/programming joke — let the punchline land as if explaining a coincidence.

phrases.text: ¿Qué hace una variable cuando se enamora? Se vuelve constante. 💕
phrases.tone: Playful, slightly romantic, with a tech pun.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between question and answer.
phrases.details: Programming love joke — let the punchline land sweetly.

phrases.text: ¿Por qué el programador se sentó frente a la pantalla? Para ver el código bien de cerca.
phrases.tone: Playful, slightly absurd, with a simple punchline.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between question and answer.
phrases.emphasis: "sentó frente a la pantalla" and "bien de cerca" (the punchline).
phrases.details: Silly programmer joke — the punchline is the absurdity. Smile at the end.

phrases.text: Oro parece, plata no es. ¿Qué es? ¡Un plátano! 🍌
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between riddle and answer.
phrases.emphasis: "Oro parece, plata no es" and "plátano" (the reveal).
phrases.pauses: Beat between the riddle and the answer; longer on the answer.
phrases.details: Classic Spanish riddle. The answer is unexpected — let the reveal land with a smile.

phrases.text: Tiene dientes y no come. Tiene cabeza y no es hombre. ¿Qué es? ¡El ajo! 🧄
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between riddle and answer.
phrases.details: Build the clues slowly. The garlic answer is the surprise — smile when delivering.

phrases.text: Vuela sin alas, silba sin boca y no se toca. ¿Qué es? ¡El viento! 💨
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between riddle and answer.
phrases.details: Poetic riddle. The wind answer is calming — let the reveal feel like an exhale.

phrases.text: Cuanto más grande, menos se ve. ¿Qué es? ¡La oscuridad! 🌑
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between riddle and answer.
phrases.emphasis: "más grande, menos se ve" and "oscuridad" (the reveal).
phrases.details: Paradox riddle. The answer is poetic — let it land with wonder.

phrases.text: Blanca por dentro, verde por fuera. ¿Qué es? ¡Una pera! 🍐
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between riddle and answer.
phrases.details: Friendly riddle. The pear answer is the surprise — let the reveal feel like a wink.

phrases.text: ¿Sabías que el primer bug de la historia fue una polilla real que se metió en una computadora en 1947? ¡De ahí viene la palabra 'bug' en programación! 🦋
phrases.tone: Didactic, enthusiastic, like a kid-friendly science show.
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a beat between the question and the answer.
phrases.details: Tech history fact. The moth visual is the hook — let "bug" land as the payoff.

phrases.text: La primera programadora del mundo fue Ada Lovelace, en 1843. ¡Hace más de 180 años! 👩‍💻
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with emphasis on the timeline.
phrases.details: Role-model fact. The time gap ("más de 180 años") is the wow moment — emphasize it.

phrases.text: El lenguaje de programación más usado del mundo se llama JavaScript. Está en casi todas las páginas web. 💻
phrases.rhythm: Medium, measured.
phrases.details: Everyday relevance — JavaScript is on the screen they're looking at.

phrases.text: Internet pesa: si cada email fuera un grano de arena, llenarían varias playas. 🏖️
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with a build to the visual.
phrases.details: Scale-of-the-internet fact. The beach image is the hook — let it paint a picture.

phrases.text: El emoji más usado del mundo es la carita que se ríe. 😂
phrases.rhythm: Medium, with emphasis on the punchline.
phrases.details: Self-referential — the kid is probably using that emoji right now. Smile with the reveal.
